I am 62 years old, and I have worked this land for 40 years. My wife and I are the only ones left at home, so I must be careful with labor. I know every inch of my 16.1 mu. This year, I will keep 6 mu in cotton because the price has been acceptable and I understand the crop, but cotton is heavy work—hand-picking every boll, spraying again and again. The remaining 10.1 mu will stay in my wheat-maize double crop, which is my backbone. The wheat gets a government subsidy, and both wheat and maize can be harvested by machine, which saves my back and fits our two-person household. I have well water, so I can irrigate when the rain fails, but pumping costs diesel and electricity, so I never water more than the crop truly needs.

For the winter wheat, I will sow an improved variety I have trusted for years. I will rotary-till the field before planting and apply 16 kg of nitrogen, 7 kg of phosphorus, and 5 kg of potassium per mu. I will irrigate three times—once before winter to protect the seedlings, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I will spray twice: once with herbicide after sowing, and once for insects and disease in spring. I expect about 520 kg per mu if the spring weather holds.

For the summer maize, I will plant hybrid seed immediately after the wheat comes off in early June. I will use no-tillage planting to save time and keep soil moisture, applying 16 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. I will irrigate twice if the summer rains are normal, and spray twice for weeds and corn borers. I expect about 600 kg per mu.

For the cotton, I will deep-plough in spring and plant a hybrid Bt cotton to resist bollworm. Cotton needs more potassium for the bolls, so I will apply 14 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 8 kg potassium per mu. I will irrigate three times during the dry spells in mid-summer, and spray four times for aphids and other secondary pests. I expect about 280 kg of seed cotton per mu.
